qAndA.answer: Some of the names included "The One Thing," "The Essence," "The Philosopher's Stone," "The Stone of Wisdom," "The Heavenly Balm," "The Divine Water," "The Virgin Water," "The Carbuncle of the Sun," "The Gold Dragon," "The Lion," "The Basilisk," and "The Phoenix."
qAndA.question: What were some of the names given to the mystical "something" sought by alchemists?

qAndA.answer: They called it the "soul of all things."
qAndA.question: According to the alchemists, what is the essential character of the object of their search?

qAndA.answer: The order was Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus, Mercury, and Luna.
qAndA.question: In what order did one alchemist arrange the seven planets?

qAndA.answer: The video explains that the process mirrors the germination of a plant seed: it needs to descend (be destroyed) before it can ascend (become life-producing).
qAndA.question: How is the process of "quickening" the seed of metals compared to a natural phenomenon?

qAndA.answer: Venus (copper) cannot be transformed into Mars (iron) due to the hierarchical order of planets.
qAndA.question: Which metal, according to the alchemists, cannot be transformed into another?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The central quest of Alchemy was the quest of an undefined and undefined a ball, something
wherein was supposed to be contained all the powers and potencies of life and whatever makes life worth living.
The names given to this mystical something were as many as the properties which were assigned to it.
It was called the one thing, the essence, the philosopher's stone, the stone of wisdom,
the heavenly balm, the divine water, the virgin water, the carbuncle of the sun,
the old dragon, the lion, the basilisk, the phoenix, and many other names were given to it.
We may come near to expressing the alchemist's view of the essential character of the object of
their search by naming it the soul of all things. Alchemy, a modern writer says, is the science of
the soul of all things. The essence was supposed to have a material form, an ethereal or middle nature,
and an immaterial or spiritual life. No one might hope to make this essence from any one
substance because, as one of the alchemists says, quote, it is the attribute of God alone to make one
out of one. You must produce one thing out of two by natural generation.
The alchemists did not pretend to create gold, but only to produce it from other things.
The author of a brief guide to the celestial ruby says, quote, we do not, as it sometimes said,
profess to create gold and silver, but only to find an agent which is capable of entering into
an intimate and maturing union with the mercury of the base metals. And quote, and again quote,
our art only aerogates to itself the power of developing through the removal of all defects
and superfluities, the golden nature which the baser metals possess. And quote,
bonus in his tract on the new pearl of great price in the 16th century says, quote, the art of alchemy
does not create metals or even develop them out of the metallic first substance. It only takes up
the unfinished handicraft of nature and completes it. Nature has only left a comparatively small thing
for the artist to do the completion of that which she has already begun. And quote,
if the essence were ever attained, it would be by following the course which nature follows in
producing the perfect plant from the imperfect seed by discovering and separating the seed of
metals and bringing that seed under the conditions which alone are suitable for its growth.
Metals must have seed. The alchemists said, for it would be absurd to suppose they have none.
What prerogative have vegetables above metals exclaims one of them that God should give seed to the
one and withhold it from the other. Are not metals as much in his sight as trees?
As metals then possess seed, it is evident how this seed is to be made active.
The seed of a plant is quickened by descending into the earth. Therefore the seed of metals
must be destroyed before it becomes life-producing.
Quote, the processes of our art must begin with dissolution of gold. They must terminate in a restoration
of the essential quality of gold. Gold does not easily give up its nature and will fight for its life,
but our agent is strong enough to overcome and kill it. And then it also has power to restore it to
life and to change the lifeless remains into a new and pure body. End quote.
The application of the doctrine of the existence of seed in metals led to the performance of many
experiments and hence to the accumulation of a considerable body of facts established by experimental
inquiries. The belief of the alchemists that all natural events are connected by a hidden thread
that everything has an influence on other things, that what is above is as what is below,
constrained them to place stress on the supposed connection between the plants and the metals.
And to further their metallic transformations by performing them at times when certain planets
were in conjunction. The seven principal planets and the seven principal metals were also called
by the same names, Sol, Gold, Luna, Silver, Saturn, Lead, Jupiter, Tin, Mars, Iron, Venus,
Copper, and Mercury. Mercury. The author of the new chemical light taught that one metal could be
propagated from another only in the order of superiority of the planets. He placed the seven
planets in the following descending order. Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Soul, Venus, Mercury, Luna.
Quote. The virtues of the planets descend, he said, but do not ascend.
It is easy to change Mars, Iron, into Venus, Copper, for instance, but Venus cannot be transformed
into Mars.

The central quest of alchemy was the quest of an undefined and undefinable something wherein was supposed to be contained all the powers and potencies of life, and whatever makes life worth living.

The names given to this mystical something were as many as the properties which were assigned to it. It was called the one thing, the essence, the philosopher's stone, the stone of wisdom, the heavenly balm, the divine water, the virgin water, the carbuncle of the sun, the old dragon, the lion, the basilisk, the phoenix; and many other names were given to it.

We may come near to expressing the alchemist's view of the essential character of the object of their search by naming it the soul of all things. "Alchemy," a modern writer says, "is the science of the soul of all things."

The essence was supposed to have a material form, an ethereal or middle nature, and an immaterial or spiritual life.
